items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.title: [meatingplace.com] H5N1 detections hit 40 Washington dairy herds as cases surge
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Bird flu spread quickly through Central Washington dairy farms in October, with 40 Washington herds testing positive from Oct. 7 to Oct. 30, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture; 33 were in Yakima County and one was in neighboring Benton County. Officials confirmed the first two cases at Yakima County dairies on Oct. 8 and four additional cases on Oct. 29. A Yakima County resident exposed to infected dairy cattle died Nov. 1, and local officials also reported two other human infections linked to cattle. Containing the virus is difficult because cattle farms cannot be sealed and controlled as tightly as poultry barns, said Rick Naerbout, executive director of the Washington State Dairy Federation. The federation advised farmers on Oct. 4 to follow biosecurity plans and alert veterinarians to falling milk production; researchers have not established the virus’s natural route of spread among cows. Washington officials say infected cows generally recover within four to six weeks, and state agriculture officials say pasteurized milk remains safe.

items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.content_html:

Data-center construction is creating union jobs in Nevada, while automation cuts or threatens positions in hospitality and customer service and employers in other sectors increase output without expanding headcount. A report by the Maine Center for Economic Policy found little evidence of widespread AI-related job losses in the state so far, while a survey of Swiss finance chiefs found 64% expect fewer entry-level finance jobs over the next three years. In Nevada, self-driving vehicles, casino robots and digital guest services are changing work on the Las Vegas Strip as thousands of tradespeople build data centers near Reno. Analysts and researchers warn that companies may reduce junior hiring because AI handles basic tasks that traditionally helped new workers gain experience. A survey cited by MIT Technology Review Insights found 16% of respondents saw transformative value from AI, while 12% had agents in production. U.S. federal AI regulation remains stalled in Congress, but a local report said the next Congress could take it up in January. China’s State Council issued guidance on Oct. 23 to limit employment displacement and support worker transitions.

items.title: [bleepingcomputer.com] Hackers used employee access and wallet authorization to steal $6.34 billion from Binance
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said attackers spent months compromising employee computers, then used stolen credentials and a wallet authorization mechanism to bypass normal transfer controls and steal about $6.34 billion on Oct. 29. The FBI attributed the operation to North Korean-linked hackers; North Korea denied responsibility. Binance traced the intrusion to a June infection through a tampered Homebrew installer, followed in September by a fake recruitment process that led another engineer to run a malicious coding assignment. The malware replaced a legitimate development component and evaded endpoint security. By Oct. 20, attackers were using a compromised computer and an internal AI tool to access two wallet engineers’ systems. On Oct. 29, attackers used a stolen deployment token to run a script and exploit Ethereum’s EIP-7702 authorization feature. Binance said the wallet’s multiparty-computation design meant no single private key could immediately revoke the authorization, requiring it to develop a special procedure. The exchange said it cleared the delegation at 00:10 UTC on Oct. 30. Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool and commissioned independent cybersecurity experts to review the breach.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian police suspend use of Crime Stoppers after 1.5 million records exposed
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

🌾 ✏️

A surprising new study suggests that eating peanuts every day could help support brain health and memory in older adults. Researchers found that consuming about two servings of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts daily for 16 weeks improved insulin responsiveness in brain regions important for memory, a function that often weakens with age and has been linked to Alzheimer's disease.

items.title: [sci.news] Cambridge study finds comets rarely delivered life’s ingredients to Earth
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

A University of Cambridge-led study finds it was extremely unlikely that comets delivered enough hydrogen cyanide, a chemical used in proposed pathways to life, to early Earth. The study, published in Scientific Reports on Oct. 28, used computer simulations to model comet evolution, atmospheric entry and impacts. The team says most impacts would destroy the molecule or fail to leave it at a useful concentration. Of the researchers’ 100,000 simulated histories, 54% included no comet impact that delivered hydrogen cyanide at concentrations considered sufficient for prebiotic chemistry. Comet delivery was more likely on Mars, where lower gravity and a thinner atmosphere make successful impacts more feasible, but the study does not establish that it happened there. The authors point to asteroid impacts or chemical processes on Earth as alternatives; outside researchers say the findings test a specific delivery pathway, not every possible comet contribution.

Possible terrestrial settings: Volcanoes and hydrothermal vents are among the proposed sources of organic precursors on Earth (sciencenews.org).

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

items.title: [americanagnetwork.com] USDA moves nearly $4 million to expand Kansas meat processing
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The U.S. Department of Agriculture is moving forward with nearly $4 million in grants to 10 Kansas meat processors to expand capacity and give livestock producers more local processing options. The funding is part of a $57.4 million round covering 147 awards in 40 states through the Meat and Poultry Processing Expansion Program. USDA said it can begin obligating the grants after completing the congressional notification period. The largest Kansas grant, $2 million for Plainview Beef Company in Peabody, will help renovate and equip a processing facility, including cold storage, packaging, rendering and wastewater systems. USDA says the projects aim to expand market access for independent producers and increase competition among processors. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said, “A strong, independent processing sector is essential to our food security, and these Kansas processors build the resilient supply chain this country needs”.
